findings.title: Constructor null-checks grantType instead of rawTokenId
findings.body: AccessTokenContext's constructor calls Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed") after already checking grantType, and never checks rawTokenId. A null raw token id is therefore stored. encodeTokenId concatenates it with ':', which Java turns into the literal suffix ":null", so every such token shares the same jti suffix and the guard the error message describes is not actually enforced.

findings.title: Access-token id matcher checks the wrong slice and inverts the result
findings.body: isAccessTokenId is what expectCodeToToken, expectRefresh, expectDeviceCodeToToken, and expectAuthReqIdToToken now use to assert Details.TOKEN_ID. The encoded id is six characters then a colon: session type [0,2), token type [2,4), grant shortcut [4,6). The matcher uses items[0].substring(3, 5), which is the last character of the token-type shortcut plus the first character of the grant shortcut (for a normal id such as onrtac this is "ta", never the grant shortcut). It also returns false when that slice equals the expected shortcut, so a correct comparison would reject valid tokens. As written, any "<prefix>:<uuid>" passes regardless of grant shortcut, and a prefix shorter than 5 characters throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException instead of failing the assertion. The new integration assertions do not actually verify the grant encoded into the access-token id.

findings.title: Grant shortcuts are not required to be exactly two characters
findings.body: postInit records each OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut() with no length or character check, and the hot-deploy refresh in getShortcutByGrantType/getGrantTypeByShortcut does the same. The default encoder just concatenates session shortcut + token-type shortcut + grant shortcut, while getTokenContextFromTokenId requires the prefix before ':' to be exactly 6 characters and otherwise throws IllegalArgumentException. OAuth2GrantTypeFactory's javadoc says the shortcut is "usually like 3-letters", which contradicts that layout. A custom grant (or a future built-in) that follows the javadoc will still issue access tokens, but those jti values can never be decoded by the default provider, so the session/token/grant context this PR adds for introspection and similar endpoints is unusable and can surface as a runtime exception.
